Use case: Shop staff can open the admin website and sign in.
What to do: 1. Open the admin website link (the HTTPS address you were given). 2. Enter the shop email and password. 3. Sign in.
What you should see: You land on the Dashboard. You can open the menu (Dashboard, Orders, Reports, Products, Customers). Sign out at the bottom of the menu when you finish on a shared computer.

Use case: A customer phone login cannot be used as shop admin.
What to do: Try to sign in with an account that is not set up as shop admin (or a wrong password).
What you should see: You see a clear “Not authorized” message. You do not see orders, customers, or sales.

Use case: The shop can see today’s work at a glance.
What to do: After sign-in, look at the four cards: Orders today, Sales today, Delivered today, and Outstanding.
What you should see: The numbers match orders you know about for today (India time). If money is still owed, Outstanding is highlighted. Tap Outstanding to open Reports.

Use case: The shop is reminded when new orders are waiting.
What to do: When at least one order is still “Placed”, look at the top of the Dashboard.
What you should see: A banner says how many orders are waiting to be confirmed. Tap it. The Orders list opens already on the Placed tab.

Use case: The shop can add a product customers can buy.
What to do: 1. Open Products. 2. Tap Add product. 3. Add a photo, name, and price. 4. Save.
What you should see: The product appears in the list as Active and Available. Later, the customer app shows it with an Add button.

Use case: The shop can hide a product or mark it not ready to buy.
What to do: On the product list: set one product to Inactive. Set another to Coming soon. Try to delete a product that was already ordered.
What you should see: Inactive products disappear from the customer app. Coming soon still shows but looks dimmed and cannot be added to the cart. A product that was ordered cannot be deleted; Inactive is the way to hide it.

Use case: The shop can group products (for example Sweets, Oils).
What to do: 1. Products → Categories. 2. Turn categories on. 3. Add a category with a name and picture. 4. Put a product in that category.
What you should see: On the customer Home screen, chips appear under search (All, then your categories). Tapping a chip filters products.

Use case: The shop can load many products from a spreadsheet.
What to do: 1. On Products, tap Export template. 2. Fill a few rows (name, price, image). 3. Choose CSV and Import.
What you should see: You see how many were imported and how many were skipped. If some rows fail, Download error log explains why. At most 250 products per file.

Use case: The shop can add a customer who ordered by phone.
What to do: 1. Open Customers → Add customer. 2. Enter name and 10-digit mobile. 3. Save. Then try the same mobile again.
What you should see: The customer is saved as Phone / Offline. The second time, the screen says the mobile already exists and offers to open that customer.

Use case: The shop can keep up to three addresses and delivery notes.
What to do: Open a customer. Add or edit an address. Add delivery instructions. Set one address as default. Try a fourth address.
What you should see: You can save at most 3 addresses. Instructions are visible to the shop. The default address is the one used next time.

Use case: The shop cannot erase a customer who already has orders.
What to do: Try Delete customer on someone with orders, and on someone with no orders.
What you should see: A customer with orders cannot be deleted. A customer with no orders can be deleted.

Use case: The shop can type a phone or walk-in order.
What to do: 1. Orders → Create order. 2. Pick or add a customer and address. 3. Add products and quantities. 4. Choose Cash, UPI, or Not yet. 5. Create order.
What you should see: A new order appears. It is marked Phone / Offline. Prices match the product list. Coming soon or inactive products cannot be added.

Use case: The shop can find orders and download a list.
What to do: On Orders, use the status tabs (All, Placed, Confirmed, and so on). Search by order number, name, or phone. Set a date filter. Tap Export.
What you should see: The list matches the filters. Export downloads a spreadsheet of those orders. You can move to the next page when there are more than 25.

Use case: The shop confirms a new customer order.
What to do: Open an order that is Placed. Tap Confirm order and confirm the question.
What you should see: Status becomes Confirmed. The customer app shows Confirmed (and a phone notification if alerts are on).

Use case: The shop can change items before the order goes out.
What to do: On a Placed or Confirmed order, tap Modify order. Add, remove, or change quantities. Review and update. Optionally add a short note.
What you should see: The customer sees “Shop modified” until they open View changes. The customer’s own 5-change limit is not used up by this shop edit.

Use case: The shop sends the order out and marks it delivered.
What to do: On the same order: Mark out for delivery, then Mark as delivered. When asked about payment, choose Cash, UPI, or Not yet.
What you should see: Each step shows a date and time. The customer sees the same steps. If you chose Not yet, the order is still unpaid (outstanding).

Use case: The shop can undo a wrong status click.
What to do: Open the … menu → Fix a status mistake. Pick the correct status and save.
What you should see: The order shows the corrected status. The customer app matches.

Use case: The shop can cancel an order and must say why.
What to do: Open … → Cancel order. Pick a reason (or Other and type a short note).
What you should see: The order is Cancelled. The customer sees it as cancelled with that reason. If it was already paid, it shows Refund pending.

Use case: The shop records cash or UPI after delivery.
What to do: Find a delivered order that is not paid. Tap Collect, choose Cash or UPI, and mark paid.
What you should see: It no longer shows as money owed. Reports Outstanding drops by that amount.

Use case: The shop can correct a payment entered by mistake.
What to do: On a paid order, open … → Change payment method. Switch Cash and UPI, or choose Not yet.
What you should see: The payment line matches what you chose. Not yet puts the amount back into outstanding.

Use case: The shop records a refund after a paid order is cancelled.
What to do: On a cancelled order that was paid, return the money outside the app, then tap Mark refunded.
What you should see: The order shows Refunded. It is not listed as outstanding.

Use case: The shop can see who still owes money.
What to do: Open Reports. Look at the Outstanding section.
What you should see: Every delivered order that is not paid is listed with the customer, phone, and amount. The total matches the Dashboard outstanding figure.

Use case: The shop can look at sales for a chosen period.
What to do: On Reports, try Today, Last 7 days, and Last 30 days. Filter by status or payment if you want.
What you should see: The summary cards (orders, sales, collected, outstanding) change to match the period. Cancelled orders are not counted in sales.

Use case: The customer’s phone alerts them when the shop moves the order.
What to do: With notifications allowed on the customer phone, change an order status in admin (for example Confirm).
What you should see: The customer’s phone shows an order update. Opening it relates to that order.

Use case: The shop can see a history of important changes.
What to do: Open Audit log. Filter last 7 days, then admin panel only, then delivery app only.
What you should see: Each row shows when, which app, and a short summary. Order lines open that order.

Use case: The shop can group addresses (for example one apartment). Customers never see this.
What to do: Customers → Communities → turn on. Create a community. Map a customer’s address to it.
What you should see: Orders for that address can be filtered as that community. The customer app does not show the community name.

Use case: The shop name and pictures match the customer app.
What to do: Open Settings (business info / branding). Check name, logo, and home banner match what you expect. Save a small change if you are allowed to test.
What you should see: The customer app welcome and home screen show the same business name and pictures after you refresh the app.

Use case: Staff can use the admin site on a phone.
What to do: Open the admin site on a phone browser. Tap Menu. Open Dashboard, Orders, and Reports.
What you should see: Lists show as cards you can tap. You can open an order without sideways scrolling. Heavy work (product import) is easier on a laptop.

Use case: A visitor can look at products before signing in.
What to do: Open the customer app. On the first screen, tap Skip. Browse Home.
What you should see: Products are visible. When you try to place an order, open Orders, or save an address, the app asks you to sign in.

Use case: A customer signs in with their mobile number.
What to do: 1. Enter the 10-digit mobile (+91 is already shown). 2. Tap Continue. 3. Enter the 6-digit code from SMS. 4. Tap Verify.
What you should see: You are signed in. In admin → Customers, this person appears with source App (first time).

Use case: A real customer receives the SMS code (after go-live SMS is turned on).
What to do: Use a normal mobile number that is not the practice test number. Request the code.
What you should see: An SMS arrives. Entering the code signs you in. Do this only after the shop has switched on real SMS.

Use case: If the SMS is late, the customer can ask again.
What to do: Tap Resend OTP. If you tap too many times quickly, read the message.
What you should see: A new code can be sent. If you are too fast, the app says to wait about a minute.

Use case: A customer saves where the order should be delivered.
What to do: Add an address: house/flat, area, 6-digit pincode, label (Home/Work/Other), receiver name and phone. Save up to 3. Try a fourth.
What you should see: City and state fill in from the pincode. You cannot save a fourth address until you delete one. The address you pick becomes the default.

Use case: A customer finds a product and adds it.
What to do: On Home, search by name. If categories exist, tap a chip. Tap Add, then use + and −.
What you should see: A green View cart bar shows how many items are in the cart. Prices look correct.

Use case: A product that is not ready cannot be bought.
What to do: Find a Coming soon product.
What you should see: It looks dimmed and says Coming soon. There is no Add button (there may be Notify me). It cannot go into the cart.

Use case: A customer can ask to be told when a Coming soon item is for sale.
What to do: On a Coming soon product, tap Notify me. Later the shop marks it Available.
What you should see: The button shows you are signed up. When the shop turns the product on, you may get a phone alert (if that feature is on).

Use case: A returning customer can reorder usual items.
What to do: Open the Order again tab.
What you should see: You see products from recent orders (cancelled orders are ignored). You can search and add them to the cart.

Use case: The cart has sensible limits.
What to do: Try to add more than 15 different products, or more than 10 of one product. Use Clear cart.
What you should see: The app explains the limit in plain words. Clear cart asks you to confirm, then empties the cart.

Use case: A customer can remove one item from the cart.
What to do: Swipe an item left and tap the bin, or reduce the quantity below 1.
What you should see: That item leaves the cart. The total updates.

Use case: The customer cannot place an order if an item became Coming soon.
What to do: Add a product, then have the shop mark it Coming soon, then try Place order.
What you should see: The app asks you to remove that item before you can place the order.

Use case: A customer places an order to be paid on delivery.
What to do: 1. Check Deliver to at the top of the cart. 2. Tap Place order (phone must be online).
What you should see: You see a thank-you screen with the order number and the amount to pay. Your Orders lists the new order. Pay on delivery is cash or UPI only.

Use case: The same house cannot have two open orders at once.
What to do: While an order is still Placed or Confirmed for an address, try to start another order to that same address.
What you should see: The app explains there is already an active order and offers View / Modify. You can deliver a new order to a different address.

Use case: Two addresses can each have their own open order.
What to do: Save two addresses. Place one open order on each.
What you should see: Both orders show under Your Orders and stay separate.

Use case: Once an order is on the way, the customer can order again to that address.
What to do: When the first order is Out for delivery, start another order for the same address.
What you should see: The screen says an order is on the way and still lets you deliver a new order there.

Use case: A customer can change an open order.
What to do: On a Placed or Confirmed order, tap Modify. Change items. Tap Update order. Also try Discard and Exit.
What you should see: You see “Order updated successfully”. Discard puts the order back. Exit leaves without saving if you confirm. You cannot modify after Out for delivery.

Use case: A customer can change one order only five times.
What to do: Modify the same order until the app stops you.
What you should see: After 5 updates it says the modify limit is reached. If the order is still Placed, it also says you can still cancel.

Use case: A customer can cancel only before the shop confirms.
What to do: On a Placed order, tap Cancel and confirm. Then try cancel on a Confirmed order.
What you should see: The Placed order becomes Cancelled. After the shop confirms, Cancel is gone. The customer can still call the shop.

Use case: A customer cannot cancel more than three orders in a day.
What to do: Cancel three orders in 24 hours, then try a fourth (all while still Placed).
What you should see: The fourth time the app says the cancel limit for today is reached and to contact the shop. Shop cancellations do not count toward this limit.

Use case: The customer can see what the shop changed.
What to do: After the shop edits items, open the order and tap View changes.
What you should see: You see what was added, removed, or changed in quantity, and the old and new total. The “Shop modified” mark goes away after you view it.

Use case: If the shop sends the order out while the customer is still editing, the edit is dropped.
What to do: Start Modify, then have the shop mark Out for delivery before Update order.
What you should see: The app explains the order is already on the way (or cancelled/delivered) and that your unsaved changes were not kept.

Use case: The customer can follow the order step by step.
What to do: Open an order from Your Orders.
What you should see: You see Order number, status, items, address, and steps: Placed, Confirmed, Out for delivery, Delivered, each with date and time when the shop recorded it. The list itself does not show the order number; the detail screen does.

Use case: The customer can pay by UPI when the order is on the way.
What to do: When status is Out for delivery and not yet paid, open the order.
What you should see: If the shop uploaded a UPI QR, you see Pay by UPI with that QR. Payment is still collected in person (cash or UPI), not inside the app.

Use case: The customer’s phone tells them the order moved.
What to do: Allow notifications. Have the shop confirm or deliver the order.
What you should see: A notification arrives for that order.

Use case: Without internet, the customer can look but not place an order.
What to do: Turn on airplane mode after you have used the app once. Browse. Try Place order.
What you should see: You see that you are offline. Saved products can stay in the cart. Placing an order, signing in, and loading Your Orders need the internet.

Use case: A first-time open with no internet shows a simple offline screen.
What to do: Install or clear the app, stay offline, and open it.
What you should see: A full “You are Offline” screen appears with Reload.

Use case: The customer can see their account and sign out.
What to do: Tap the round initial on Home. Check name, mobile, and address. Tap Sign out.
What you should see: Account details look right. After sign out you must sign in again to order.

App category: Order app → Admin panel → Delivery app
Use case: One real order goes from the customer all the way to paid.
What to do: 1. Customer places an order. 2. Shop confirms, sends it out, and marks delivered. 3. Record Cash or UPI (admin website or delivery app).
What you should see: The customer sees Delivered. Reports no longer shows that order as unpaid. This is the main check before launch.

Use case: A driver signs in with the same shop login as the website.
What to do: Open the delivery app. Enter the admin email and password (not a customer mobile code).
What you should see: Today’s deliveries opens.

Use case: The driver sees what still needs delivering today.
What to do: Look at To deliver and Delivered today.
What you should see: To deliver shows orders that are Placed, Confirmed, or Out for delivery. Delivered today shows orders marked delivered today (India time).

Use case: The driver moves the order forward from the phone.
What to do: Open an order. Swipe through Confirm, Start delivery, and Mark delivered as the buttons allow.
What you should see: The website and the customer app show the same new status.

Use case: The driver records how the customer paid at the door.
What to do: When marking Delivered, choose Cash, UPI, or Not yet.
What you should see: Cash or UPI clears the amount owed. Not yet leaves it outstanding on the website Reports.

Use case: The driver can show the shop UPI QR.
What to do: On an unpaid delivery, show the UPI QR. If you are allowed, upload or replace the QR photo.
What you should see: The customer app shows the same QR when the order is out for delivery and unpaid.

Use case: If the website already marked the order delivered, the phone does not deliver it twice.
What to do: Mark Delivered on the admin website, then open the same order in the delivery app.
What you should see: The app refreshes. You are not asked to deliver again. You can still record payment if it was Not yet.

Use case: The driver can call the customer or open maps.
What to do: On an order card, tap Call and Map.
What you should see: The phone dialer opens, and maps opens for the address.

Use case: Delivery actions show up in the shop’s history.
What to do: After a delivery status change, open Audit log on the website and filter Delivery app.
What you should see: You see a row for that action from the delivery app.

Use case: After two real orders, the Play Store may ask for a rating.
What to do: On a Play Store test install (not Expo Go), place two new orders successfully.
What you should see: Google may show a rating box once. It is OK if Google chooses not to show it. The app must not crash. Check this after the app is on Play, before you advertise widely.
